cards.explanation: The priest sets a price they can afford. The person is presented before the priest, who sets the value according to what the one making the vow can afford (Leviticus 27:8). The list has prices, but it also has room for an empty pocket. Nobody gets turned away at the door of this bakery over a few missing coins.
The word is holy. Verse 9 says any such animal given to the LORD shall be holy (Leviticus 27:9). Once it's vowed, it's not just another animal in the pen anymore. It belongs to the LORD.

The answer is False. The text says, “He must not replace it or exchange it, either good for bad or bad for good.” (Leviticus 27:10) That covers swapping up as well as swapping down, friends. Once the animal is vowed, no trading.

Both of the animals end up holy. Verse 10 says, if he does substitute one animal for another, both that animal and its substitute will be holy (Leviticus 27:10). So the swap doesn't get him out of anything. It just adds a second animal to the LORD's side of the pen.

The answer is False. The animal is presented before the priest, and the priest shall set its value, whether high or low (Leviticus 27:11-12). As the priest values it, the price will be set. The owner doesn't get to haggle his own number.

The word is fifth. Verse 13 says that if the owner decides to redeem the animal, he must add a fifth to its value (Leviticus 27:13). So buying it back costs a little more than the priest's price. One more piece on top, and the animal is his again.

The priest figures the price by the years left until the next Jubilee. Verse 18 says the priest calculates the price in proportion to the years left until the next Year of Jubilee, so that the valuation will be reduced (Leviticus 27:18). Fewer years left means a lower price. It's like a lease that runs shorter every year.

No, it can no longer be redeemed. Verse 20 says that if he does not redeem the field, or if he has sold it to another man, it may no longer be redeemed (Leviticus 27:20). The door closes, and there's no knocking on it afterward. It's like a cookie sale where the last batch sells out and you're standing there with an empty box, still saying, “But I wanted one!” So the time to buy it back is while he still can.

The answer is True. Verse 21 says that when the field is released in the Jubilee, it will become holy, like a field devoted to the LORD. It becomes the property of the priests (Leviticus 27:21). This follows from verse 20, where the field was never redeemed or was sold to another man.

The field goes back to its original owner. Verse 24 says that in the Year of Jubilee the field shall return to the one from whom it was bought, the original owner of the land (Leviticus 27:24). The man consecrated a field he bought, so it goes back to where it came from.

It can't be consecrated because it already belongs to the LORD. Verse 26 says no one may consecrate a firstborn of the livestock, because a firstborn belongs to the LORD. Whether it is an ox or a sheep, it is the LORD's (Leviticus 27:26). You can't give someone something that's already theirs.

The word is sold. Verse 27 says that if the firstborn is among the unclean animals, he may redeem it according to the valuation and add a fifth of its value. If it is not redeemed, then it shall be sold according to the valuation (Leviticus 27:27). Redeem it or it's sold.

The answer is False. The fifth doesn't work here, friends. Verse 28 says that whether it's a man, an animal, or his inherited land, nothing set apart to the LORD can be sold or redeemed. Everything so devoted is most holy to the LORD (Leviticus 27:28).

The tithe belongs to the LORD. Verse 30 says any tithe from the land, whether from the seed of the land or the fruit of the trees, belongs to the LORD. It is holy to the LORD (Leviticus 27:30). The tithe is His from the start.

The word is tenth. Verse 32 says every tenth animal from the herd or flock that passes under the shepherd's rod will be holy to the LORD (Leviticus 27:32). Every tenth one that passes under the rod belongs to Him. The shepherd just keeps counting.

The answer is False. The text says, “He must not inspect whether it is good or bad, and he shall not make any substitution.” (Leviticus 27:33) No peeking, no picking, friends. The tenth animal is the tenth animal.
